claim: Functional UltraSound (fUS) is an emerging technology that offers images of cerebral blood volume over large brain portions.
source: Functional UltraSound (fUS) is an emerging technology that offers images of cerebral blood volume over large brain portions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the fUS technology.

claim: fUS provides stable (over days), yet rapid, highly-resolved 3D tonotopic maps in the auditory pathway of awake ferrets.
source: We demonstrate that fUS provides stable (over days), yet rapid, highly-resolved 3D tonotopic maps in the auditory pathway of awake ferrets, thus revealing its unprecedented functional resolution (100/300µm).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing tonotopic maps obtained over multiple days with specified resolution.

claim: fUS has an unprecedented functional resolution of 100/300µm.
source: We demonstrate that fUS provides stable (over days), yet rapid, highly-resolved 3D tonotopic maps in the auditory pathway of awake ferrets, thus revealing its unprecedented functional resolution (100/300µm).
evidence: The resolution is quantified based on experimental measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: fUS mapping was performed in four different brain regions in the ferret auditory pathway.
source: This was performed in four different brain regions, including very small (1–2 mm3 size), deeply situated subcortical (8 mm deep) and previously undescribed structures in the ferret.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that four different brain regions were mapped.

claim: Some of the mapped structures are very small (1–2 mm3 size).
source: This was performed in four different brain regions, including very small (1–2 mm3 size), deeply situated subcortical (8 mm deep) and previously undescribed structures in the ferret.
evidence: The size of structures is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Some of the mapped structures are deeply situated subcortical structures (8 mm deep).
source: This was performed in four different brain regions, including very small (1–2 mm3 size), deeply situated subcortical (8 mm deep) and previously undescribed structures in the ferret.
evidence: The depth of subcortical structures is explicitly stated.

claim: Some of the mapped structures were previously undescribed in the ferret.
source: This was performed in four different brain regions, including very small (1–2 mm3 size), deeply situated subcortical (8 mm deep) and previously undescribed structures in the ferret.
evidence: The abstract states that some structures were previously undescribed.

claim: fUS was used to map long-distance projections from frontal cortex to auditory cortex.
source: Furthermore, we used fUS to map long-distance projections from frontal cortex, a key source of sensory response modulation, to auditory cortex.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this application of fUS.

claim: Frontal cortex is a key source of sensory response modulation.
source: Furthermore, we used fUS to map long-distance projections from frontal cortex, a key source of sensory response modulation, to auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of the study.

claim: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUS) based on Ultrafast Doppler (UfD) was first introduced in neuroimaging in 2011.
source: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUS) based on Ultrafast Doppler (UfD) was first introduced in neuroimaging in 2011 (Macé et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: The fUS system exhibits a 50-fold enhanced sensitivity to blood volume changes compared to conventional ultrasound Doppler techniques.
source: Using ultrasonic plane wave emissions, this system exhibits a 50-fold enhanced sensitivity to blood volume changes compared to conventional ultrasound Doppler techniques (Mace et al., 2013), with a very high acquisition rate (ms) enabling unambiguous discrimination between blood flow and motion artifacts (breathing motion, tissue pulsatility,...) (Demené et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: fUS has a very high acquisition rate (ms) enabling unambiguous discrimination between blood flow and motion artifacts.
source: Using ultrasonic plane wave emissions, this system exhibits a 50-fold enhanced sensitivity to blood volume changes compared to conventional ultrasound Doppler techniques (Mace et al., 2013), with a very high acquisition rate (ms) enabling unambiguous discrimination between blood flow and motion artifacts (breathing motion, tissue pulsatility,...) (Demené et al., 2015).
evidence: This technical capability is stated and supported by citation.

claim: fUS presents substantially higher spatial resolution for cerebral blood flow imaging compared to fMRI.
source: Relative to fMRI, it also presents substantially higher spatial resolution for cerebral blood flow imaging at the expense of non-invasiveness, greater portability and lower cost, and versatility for awake animal imaging.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the technology's capabilities.

claim: Most fUS studies thus far have investigated its sensitivity in capturing coarse-grained sensory responses.
source: However, most fUS studies thus far have investigated its sensitivity in capturing coarse-grained sensory responses (Tiran et al., 2017; Osmanski et al., 2014a; Gesnik et al., 2017; Urban et al., 2014; Urban et al., 2015), or used it to explore indirect in-plane brain connectivity (Osmanski et al., 2014b; Rideau Batista Novais et al., 2016).
evidence: This characterization of prior work is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The theoretical spatial resolution of Ultrafast Doppler for high sensitivity mapping of microvascularisation has been shown to be 100 µm for whole brain imaging in rats.
source: Also, while the theoretical spatial resolution of Ultrafast Doppler for high sensitivity mapping of microvascularisation has been shown to be 100 µm for whole brain imaging in rats (Mace et al., 2013; Demené et al., 2016), the ability of the fUS technique to measure independent information on functional brain activity from the cerebral blood volume (CBV) variation maps at such a small scale, that is the truly informative fUS imaging resolution, has remained to date unproven.
evidence: This claim about theoretical resolution is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ability of fUS to measure independent information on functional brain activity at 100 µm scale has remained unproven prior to this study.
source: Also, while the theoretical spatial resolution of Ultrafast Doppler for high sensitivity mapping of microvascularisation has been shown to be 100 µm for whole brain imaging in rats (Mace et al., 2013; Demené et al., 2016), the ability of the fUS technique to measure independent information on functional brain activity from the cerebral blood volume (CBV) variation maps at such a small scale, that is the truly informative fUS imaging resolution, has remained to date unproven.
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Physiological experiments were conducted in three awake ferrets (Mustela putorius furo).
source: Physiological experiments were conducted in three awake ferrets (Mustela putorius furo, thereafter called V, B and S).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Craniotomies were performed over the temporal lobe and chronic imaging chambers were installed.
source: After performing craniotomies over the temporal lobe, chronic imaging chambers were installed (both hemispheres in one animal, and right hemispheres in the other two) to access a large portion of both the auditory (middle and posterior ectosylvian gyri - resp. MEG and PEG) and visual cortex (in caudal suprasylvian and lateral gyri) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation performed.

claim: The 3D scan of the craniotomy via Ultrafast Doppler Tomography revealed the in-depth vasculature of the Auditory Cortex surrounded by the supra-sylvian sulcus.
source: The 3D scan of the craniotomy via Ultrafast Doppler Tomography (Demené et al., 2016) revealed the in-depth vasculature of the Auditory Cortex (AC) surrounded by the supra-sylvian sulcus (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This describes what was observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: fUS was able to detect and image deep auditory-responsive structures such as the Medial Geniculate Body (MGB), the Inferior Colliculus (IC) and the dorsal nucleus of the Lateral Lemniscus (DNLL).
source: In addition, we were able to detect and image deep auditory-responsive structures such as the Medial Geniculate Body (MGB), the Inferior Colliculus (IC) and the dorsal nucleus of the Lateral Lemniscus (DNLL), as well as visually-responsive nuclei such as the Lateral Geniculate (LGN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the capability demonstrated in the experimental data.

claim: fUS was able to image visually-responsive nuclei such as the Lateral Geniculate (LGN).
source: In addition, we were able to detect and image deep auditory-responsive structures such as the Medial Geniculate Body (MGB), the Inferior Colliculus (IC) and the dorsal nucleus of the Lateral Lemniscus (DNLL), as well as visually-responsive nuclei such as the Lateral Geniculate (LGN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the capability demonstrated in the experimental data.

claim: Within 10 to 15 min per slice, fUS could accurately reproduce the known tonotopic organization of the primary and secondary auditory cortex.
source: Within a relatively short time (10 to 15 min per slice), we could accurately reproduce the known tonotopic organization of the primary (A1 and AAF in the middle ectosylvian gyrus) and secondary auditory cortex (PPF and PSF in the posterior ectosylvian gyrus) (Bizley et al., 2005; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2006; Nelken et al., 2008), with a high- to low-frequency gradient in A1, reversing to a low- to high-frequency gradient in the dorsal PEG (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the speed and accuracy of the mapping demonstrated in the data.

claim: A1 exhibits a high- to low-frequency gradient.
source: Within a relatively short time (10 to 15 min per slice), we could accurately reproduce the known tonotopic organization of the primary (A1 and AAF in the middle ectosylvian gyrus) and secondary auditory cortex (PPF and PSF in the posterior ectosylvian gyrus) (Bizley et al., 2005; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2006; Nelken et al., 2008), with a high- to low-frequency gradient in A1, reversing to a low- to high-frequency gradient in the dorsal PEG (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the tonotopic organization observed in the data and known from prior work.

claim: The dorsal PEG exhibits a low- to high-frequency gradient.
source: Within a relatively short time (10 to 15 min per slice), we could accurately reproduce the known tonotopic organization of the primary (A1 and AAF in the middle ectosylvian gyrus) and secondary auditory cortex (PPF and PSF in the posterior ectosylvian gyrus) (Bizley et al., 2005; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2006; Nelken et al., 2008), with a high- to low-frequency gradient in A1, reversing to a low- to high-frequency gradient in the dorsal PEG (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the tonotopic organization observed in the data.

claim: fUS enabled mapping within the challenging deep folds of the ferret auditory cortex, such as the supra-sylvian sulcus (sss) and pseudo-sylvian sulcus (pss).
source: We note that the fUS enabled us to map within the challenging deep folds of the ferret auditory cortex, such as the supra-sylvian sulcus (sss) and pseudo-sylvian sulcus (pss).
evidence: This describes a capability of the technique demonstrated in the study.

claim: Recordings could be performed in the same slice across days, with a high repositioning precision (error <1 slice, 200 µm).
source: Recordings could be performed in the same slice across days, with a high repositioning precision (error <1 slice, 200 µm in that case), which was within the range of the out-of-plane point-spread function for fUS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the reproducibility demonstrated in the experimental data.

claim: The repositioning precision was within the range of the out-of-plane point-spread function for fUS.
source: Recordings could be performed in the same slice across days, with a high repositioning precision (error <1 slice, 200 µm in that case), which was within the range of the out-of-plane point-spread function for fUS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This relates the measured precision to the technical specifications of the imaging system.

claim: fUS was able to capture inter-individual variability along the transect going from the pss to the sss, consistent with previous work in the ferret.
source: Interestingly we were able to capture inter-individual variability along the transect going from the pss to the sss, consistent with previous work in the ferret (Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a finding from the data that is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Large-scale, 3D functional maps were recorded in the deep and smaller structures of the auditory thalamus (MGB), the inferior colliculus (IC) and the DNLL.
source: Large-scale, 3D functional maps were also recorded in the deep and smaller structures of the auditory thalamus (MGB, Figure 1d), the inferior colliculus (IC, Figure 1e) and the DNLL (Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes the scope of mapping achieved in the study.

claim: The tonotopical organization of the ferret ventral division of the MGB was described for the first time using fUS.
source: The 3D views obtained in fUS allowed us to describe for the first time the tonotopical organizations of the ferret ventral division of the MGB and DNLL.
evidence: This claims a novel finding from the study.

claim: The tonotopical organization of the ferret DNLL was described for the first time using fUS.
source: The 3D views obtained in fUS allowed us to describe for the first time the tonotopical organizations of the ferret ventral division of the MGB and DNLL.
evidence: This claims a novel finding from the study.

claim: A precise tonotopic map was characterized in the DNLL despite its small size (~1 mm-long) and subcortical position (8 mm deep below brain surface).
source: This is particularly remarkable in the latter structure in which we characterize a precise tonotopic map despite its small size (~1 mm-long) and subcortical position (8 mm deep below brain surface).
evidence: This describes a specific achievement of the mapping in a challenging structure.

claim: The large field of view allows measurement of the functional organization of any coplanar structure simultaneously.
source: Moreover, such a large field of view allows one to measure simultaneously the functional organization of any coplanar structure (such as A1 and the MGB here), thus opening the door to precise, frequency specific (thalamo-cortical) connectivity studies.
evidence: This describes a capability of the technique and its implications.

claim: High decoding accuracy was attained in the auditory cortex (from 0.46 to 0.63 probability, with chance at 0.2).
source: Using a simple linear decoder, we attained high decoding accuracy in the auditory cortex (from 0.46 to 0.63 probability, with chance at 0.2) which was even more striking in the IC and DNLL (from 0.72 to 0.98), despite their smaller size and subcortical location (Figure 2a).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from the decoding analysis.

claim: Decoding accuracy was even more striking in the IC and DNLL (from 0.72 to 0.98), despite their smaller size and subcortical location.
source: Using a simple linear decoder, we attained high decoding accuracy in the auditory cortex (from 0.46 to 0.63 probability, with chance at 0.2) which was even more striking in the IC and DNLL (from 0.72 to 0.98), despite their smaller size and subcortical location (Figure 2a).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from the decoding analysis.

claim: Single trials show reliable and significant activity across all structures.
source: These results suggest that single trials show reliable and significant activity across all structures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high decoding accuracy results.

claim: A linear decoder yielded significantly higher decoding accuracy when using only measurements at intermediate cortical depths (p<1e-3), peaking around 400–500 µm below the surface.
source: A linear decoder yielded a significantly higher decoding accuracy when using only measurements at intermediate cortical depths (p<1e-3), peaking around 400–500 µm below the surface (up to 0.83, mean 0.67), consistent with it being granular.
evidence: This reports a statistical finding from the depth-dependent analysis.

claim: The peak in decoding accuracy at 400-500 µm depth is consistent with this depth being granular layer.
source: A linear decoder yielded a significantly higher decoding accuracy when using only measurements at intermediate cortical depths (p<1e-3), peaking around 400–500 µm below the surface (up to 0.83, mean 0.67), consistent with it being granular.
evidence: This interprets the depth finding in terms of cortical layer anatomy.

claim: Baseline blood volume and response magnitude did not show a similar depth-dependent profile.
source: As a control, we note that baseline blood volume and response magnitude did not show a similar depth-dependent profile (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed decoding accuracy may be due to variations in capillaries structure within cortical layers (Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: This reports a control analysis to rule out alternative explanations.

claim: The observed decoding accuracy may be due to variations in capillaries structure within cortical layers.
source: As a control, we note that baseline blood volume and response magnitude did not show a similar depth-dependent profile (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed decoding accuracy may be due to variations in capillaries structure within cortical layers (Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results supported by citation.

claim: An alternative explanation for improved accuracy at intermediate depths is that it reflects the sharper frequency tuning observed in granular layers.
source: An alternative explanation would be that the improved accuracy at the intermediate depths reflects the underlying neuronal activity, and more specifically the sharper frequency tuning observed in granular layers (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: All results could be confirmed in single slice recordings, and over several days.
source: Importantly, all these results could be confirmed in single slice recordings, and over several days (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), showing that the hemodynamic signal imaged in fUS is reliable enough to decode brain activity on a single-trial basis within a single experiment.
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the findings.

claim: The hemodynamic signal imaged in fUS is reliable enough to decode brain activity on a single-trial basis within a single experiment.
source: Importantly, all these results could be confirmed in single slice recordings, and over several days (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), showing that the hemodynamic signal imaged in fUS is reliable enough to decode brain activity on a single-trial basis within a single experiment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reproducibility and decoding results.

claim: fUS can discriminate responsiveness of neighboring voxels with a functional resolution as fine as 100 µm.
source: We found that fUS can discriminate responsiveness of neighboring voxels, with a functional resolution as fine as 100 µm (Figure 2b).
evidence: This reports a quantitative finding about spatial resolution.

claim: fUS was able to discriminate voxels based on their tuning curves within a distance of 300 µm in as little as 10 repetitions per frequency.
source: Furthermore, we were able to discriminate voxels based on their tuning curves within a distance of 300 µm in as little as 10 repetitions per frequency (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports a quantitative finding about functional resolution for tuning discrimination.

claim: The functional resolution described is a conservative measure and a lower limit.
source: Importantly, this is a conservative measure of functional resolution, since it largely depends on the smoothness of the underlying functional organization itself (tonotopy) and of the number of trials. The functional resolution described here is thus a lower limit, and could be improved by increasing, for example, the trial number.
evidence: This qualifies the resolution measurements and explains their limitations.

claim: fUS can be useful to assess the fine organization of vascular domains within brain structures.
source: These results suggest that fUS can be useful to assess the fine organization of vascular domains within brain structures and to better understand the functional coupling between local neuronal activity and the dynamics of surrounding blood vessels, two important questions for hemodynamic-based techniques (O'Herron et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference about potential applications based on the demonstrated resolution.

claim: fUS can help better understand the functional coupling between local neuronal activity and the dynamics of surrounding blood vessels.
source: These results suggest that fUS can be useful to assess the fine organization of vascular domains within brain structures and to better understand the functional coupling between local neuronal activity and the dynamics of surrounding blood vessels, two important questions for hemodynamic-based techniques (O'Herron et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference about potential applications supported by citations.

claim: Localizing and quantifying connections between distant brain structures in awake animals remains technically challenging.
source: Localizing and quantifying such connections in awake animals, however, remains technically challenging since tracer injections are not an option, and fMRI gives only access to indirect, spatially diffuse measures of connectivity strength.
evidence: This describes a limitation of existing methods that motivates the current work.

claim: fUS can be used to probe the functional connectivity between the frontal and auditory cortices.
source: Here, we demonstrate that fUS can be used to probe the functional connectivity between two brain structures that are far apart: the frontal and the auditory cortices.
evidence: This describes a capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: The frontal cortex is a region involved in top-down modulation of early sensory areas, particularly the auditory cortex.
source: The frontal cortex (FC) is a region that has been shown to be involved in top-down modulation of early sensory areas, and in particular of the auditory cortex (Fritz et al., 2003; Winkowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the frontal cortex evoked activity in the insular cortex of the pseudosylvian sulcus (PSSC/insula).
source: By imaging widely in the auditory cortex, we observed evoked activity in the insular cortex of the pseudosylvian sulcus (PSSC/insula), which was maximal for a certain depth and position of the stimulating electrode (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports an experimental observation from the stimulation experiments.

claim: There was no evoked activity recorded in secondary auditory areas such as the PEG following frontal cortex stimulation.
source: By contrast, there was no evoked activity recorded in secondary auditory areas such as the PEG (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports a negative finding from the stimulation experiments.

claim: A decrease in blood volume was observed in the MEG following frontal cortex stimulation, possibly originating from polysynaptic connections between FC and A1.
source: We also observed a decrease in blood volume in the MEG, possibly originating from polysynaptic connections between FC and A1 (Logothetis et al., 2010; Klink et al., 2017).
evidence: This reports an observation and offers a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Anterograde virus injections in FC revealed monosynaptic projections that targeted the PSSC/insula.
source: We therefore anatomically confirmed the existence of such descending projections from FC to PSSC/insula with independent anterograde virus injections in FC. These injections revealed monosynaptic projections that targeted the PSSC/insula (Figure 3c–d), consistent with a contribution of direct projections from FC to A1 to the functional connectivity pattern revealed by the fUS approach.
evidence: This reports anatomical confirmation of the functional connectivity findings.

claim: FC projections were also observed in the Claustrum, ventro-medial with respect to the PSSC/insula.
source: We also observed FC projections in the Claustrum (Cl in Figure 3c), ventro-medial with respect to the PSSC/insula.
evidence: This reports an additional anatomical observation.

claim: The FC-targeted PSSC/insula region was less responsive to broadband noise than A1 (~5% instead of 15%).
source: We found this region to be less responsive to broadband noise than A1 (~5% instead of 15%), and not driven by visual stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports a quantitative comparison of sensory responses.

claim: The FC-targeted PSSC/insula region was not driven by visual stimuli.
source: We found this region to be less responsive to broadband noise than A1 (~5% instead of 15%), and not driven by visual stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports a finding about sensory modality specificity.

claim: fUS can serve as a tool to characterize large-scale functional connectivity without sacrificing resolution.
source: Altogether, this experiment offers a proof-of-concept of how fUS can serve as a tool to characterize large-scale functional connectivity without sacrificing any resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the connectivity experiments.

claim: fUS can be used to explore connectivity changes in animals during different brain states or during learning.
source: First, one may explore connectivity changes in animals, for example during different brain states (e.g., sleep vs. awake), or during the course of learning.
evidence: This proposes a potential application based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: The use of optogenetics with fUS can allow precise mapping between brain structures, targeting specific neuronal subpopulations or projection patterns.
source: Second, and maybe even more importantly, the use of optogenetics can allow a precise mapping between brain structures, targeting for example specific neuronal subpopulations, or projection patterns.
evidence: This proposes a potential future application combining fUS with optogenetics.

claim: The amplitude of fUS responses is ~20% in the ferret and close to 50% in neonates.
source: The amplitude of the fUS responses (~20% in the ferret, and close to 50% in neonates [Demene et al., 2017]) is quite large compared to typical auditory cortex BOLD responses in fMRI (~5%).
evidence: This reports quantitative measurements of response amplitudes with citation for neonates.

claim: Typical auditory cortex BOLD responses in fMRI are ~5%.
source: The amplitude of the fUS responses (~20% in the ferret, and close to 50% in neonates [Demene et al., 2017]) is quite large compared to typical auditory cortex BOLD responses in fMRI (~5%).
evidence: This provides a comparison value for fMRI responses.

claim: The large amplitude of fUS responses makes mapping both rapid and precise.
source: This makes mapping both rapid, compared to the electrophysiological approach with multiple penetrations (Bizley et al., 2005; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2006), and precise, as illustrated by the ease with which single-trial information can be decoded from its high-sensitivity signal, a key feature when it comes to recording in behaving animals.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of fUS based on the response amplitude and demonstrated capabilities.

claim: fUS can be a valuable tool in acquiring broad, yet accurate views of the functional organization of unmapped brain regions and their connectivity.
source: Furthermore, fUS can be a valuable tool in acquiring broad, yet accurate views of the functional organization of unmapped brain regions and their connectivity with the rest of the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of fUS based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: fUS imaging can be readily adapted to mobile and highly stable configurations.
source: Finally, fUS imaging can be readily adapted to mobile and highly stable configurations (Sieu et al., 2015), which will make it ideally suited for behavioral cognitive neuroscience studies requiring extended observations, as in the characterization of the neural correlates of learning.
evidence: This describes a technical capability supported by citation.

claim: fUS is ideally suited for behavioral cognitive neuroscience studies requiring extended observations.
source: Finally, fUS imaging can be readily adapted to mobile and highly stable configurations (Sieu et al., 2015), which will make it ideally suited for behavioral cognitive neuroscience studies requiring extended observations, as in the characterization of the neural correlates of learning.
evidence: This is an inference about future applications based on the technical capabilities.

claim: Experiments were approved by the French Ministry of Agriculture (protocol authorization: 01236.02).
source: Experiments were approved by the French Ministry of Agriculture (protocol authorization: 01236.02) and strictly comply with the European directives on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (2010/63/EU).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The experiments strictly comply with the European directives on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (2010/63/EU).
source: Experiments were approved by the French Ministry of Agriculture (protocol authorization: 01236.02) and strictly comply with the European directives on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes (2010/63/EU).
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory compliance.

claim: A custom miniaturized probe with 15 MHz central frequency, 70% bandwidth, 0.110 mm pitch, and 128 elements was used.
source: We used a custom miniaturized probe (15 MHz central frequency, 70% bandwidth, 0.110 mm pitch, 128 elements) inserted in a four degree-of-freedom motorized setup.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the imaging probe.

claim: UFD-T acquires 2D Ultrafast Power Doppler images at a frame rate of 500 Hz.
source: Briefly, this method acquires 2D Ultrafast Power Doppler (UfD) images at a frame rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes a technical parameter of the imaging method.

claim: UFD-T ultimately recovers an isotropic 100 µm 3D resolution.
source: Each frame is a compound frame built with 11 tilted plane wave emissions (−10° to 10° with 2° steps) fired at a PRF of 5500 Hz, combined with mechanical translation and rotation, and then post-processed via a Wiener deconvolution to correct for the intrinsic out-of-plane loss of resolution, so that we ultimately recover an isotropic 100 µm 3D resolution.
evidence: This describes the achieved spatial resolution of the 3D vascular imaging.

claim: A 3D (14 × 14 × 20 mm) blood volume reconstruction of the vasculature is obtained with voxel size of 50 µm and isotropic resolution of 100 µm.
source: In the end, a 3D (14 × 14 × 20 mm) blood volume reconstruction of the vasculature is obtained (voxel size: 50 µm, isotropic resolution 100 µm).
evidence: This describes the output specifications of the 3D vascular imaging.

claim: fUS imaging relies on rapid acquisition (every 1 s) of ultrasensitive 2D Power UfD images.
source: fUS imaging relies on rapid acquisition (every 1 s) of ultrasensitive 2D Power UfD images of the ferret brain.
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution of functional imaging.

claim: For each Power image, 300 frames are acquired at a 500 Hz frame rate.
source: For each Power image, 300 frames are acquired at a 500 Hz frame rate (covering 600ms, that is one to two ferret cardiac cycles), each frame being a compound frame acquired via 11 tilted plane wave emissions (-10° to 10° with 2° steps) fired at a PRF of 5500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the acquisition parameters for functional imaging.

claim: Power Doppler is proportional to blood volume.
source: This power Doppler is known to be proportional to blood volume (Rubin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Five equally spaced frequencies on a logarithmic scale (602 Hz, 1430 Hz, 3400 Hz, 8087 Hz, 19234 Hz) were used to map tonotopic organization.
source: To image these tonotopic maps, we played unmodulated pure tones while recording fUS images at five equally spaced frequencies on a logarithmic scale (602 Hz, 1430 Hz, 3400 Hz, 8087 Hz, 19234 Hz, covering the auditory hearing spectrum of the ferret, at 65 dBSPL).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiments.

claim: The five frequencies used cover the auditory hearing spectrum of the ferret.
source: To image these tonotopic maps, we played unmodulated pure tones while recording fUS images at five equally spaced frequencies on a logarithmic scale (602 Hz, 1430 Hz, 3400 Hz, 8087 Hz, 19234 Hz, covering the auditory hearing spectrum of the ferret, at 65 dBSPL).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the frequency selection.

claim: Unmodulated pure tone stimuli elicited large and reliable responses in the whole auditory tract.
source: We note that these tone stimuli elicited large and reliable responses in the whole auditory tract despite being unmodulated.
evidence: This is an observation about the effectiveness of the stimuli.

claim: A variety of other auditory stimuli (such as natural sounds) can be used to elicit stronger responses and reveal more organizational properties.
source: This suggests that a variety of other auditory stimuli (such as natural sounds) can be used to elicit stronger responses and hence reveal more organizational properties.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experimental possibilities based on the current findings.

claim: Frontal cortex electric stimulations consisted of monophasic stimulation at 100 Hz and 200 µA (2 ms pulses, 200ms-long train, repeated at 2 Hz).
source: Each trial consisted of 10 s of baseline, then 6 s of monophasic stimulation at 100 Hz and 200 µA (2 ms pulses, 200ms-long train, repeated at 2 Hz), after a return to baseline of 10 s.
evidence: This describes the electrical stimulation parameters used.

claim: In connectivity experiments, the animal was slightly sedated using a small dose of medetomidine (Domitor 0.02 mL at 0.08 mg.kg−1) to reduce movement artifacts.
source: In these connectivity experiments, the animal was slightly sedated using a small dose of medetomidine (Domitor 0.02 mL at 0.08 mg.kg−1) to reduce movement artifacts.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the connectivity studies.

claim: Stimulation experiments were performed in one ferret, and each of the four experiments was done once, on different days.
source: Stimulation experiments were performed in one ferret, and each of the four experiments presented (Figure 3 and its figures supplements) was done once, on different days.
evidence: This describes the sample size and experimental design for connectivity studies.
